text: A residue-scoped acknowledgement for prose-revised-since-proof

All source observations below were taken against a single, clean worktree state: branch `tet30-prose-revised-since-proof` at commit `c821b94`, the commit that shipped TET-30's `prose-revised-since-proof` residue. Nothing in this design was implemented; the tree was read, never written.
What the residue actually computes

TET-30's listing is worth restating precisely, because the acknowledgement designed here has to key on exactly the quantities the listing keys on, and no others. For each non-heading block with a non-empty citation list, the check derives an anchor — the latest moment at which any of the block's cited claims first entered proof — and a block timestamp, which is not the time of the block's last edit but the time at which the block's *current* text-and-citation pair first appeared anywhere in its history. The block is listed when the pair postdates the anchor. None of these three values is stored; all are recomputed from the event logs at check time.
Where the event lives, and what it costs

The sketch left the event's home open between `prose.jsonl` and a sibling log. The evidence closes it, and not on grounds of taste. `ProseEvent` is an internally-tagged enum over two variants, and the workspace's line reader turns any single unparseable line into an error over the entire log. A third variant is therefore not a compatible addition: I wrote a scratch workspace whose prose log held one ordinary `Create` followed by one `Ack`, and the build at this pin refused the whole file — including the `Create` it understood perfectly well. Every older build encountering such a snapshot would lose its ability to read prose at all, which is a far worse outcome than the residue line this design exists to clear. The field-level `#[serde(default)]` precedent already in both variants does not extend to a new variant.

So the event lives in its own append-only log, `acks.jsonl`, and the snapshot manifest gains a tenth entry. That manifest is an explicit enumeration precisely so that shipping a new workspace file is a decision rather than an accident, and it is what makes the cross-build story tolerable: a build predating the entry never opens the file, reads the prose log unchanged, and prints exactly the listing TET-30 shipped. The degradation is one-directional — an older build over-reports an entry a newer build would suppress, and can never suppress one an older build would show. That is the direction a silent-by-default, human-owed residue should fail in.
The residue nobody can honestly clear

TET-30 names two acts that clear a listing, and for the case this design is about — an edit that corrects the prose and touches no claim's proposition — both of them lie. Restoring the text puts the typo back. Revising a correct claim so that its new wording can be graded is worse than expensive: because out-of-proof is one of the machine-check disjuncts and this residue is not, that route turns a green run red, and keeps it red until another grounding pass lands, in order to silence a line that by construction never failed anything. An author who reads their paragraph against its claims, finds the paragraph faithful, and has nothing to change is left with no act at all. That is the defect: not the listing on first appearance, which is informative, but its permanence after the human act it asks for has been performed.
What the reader sees

The brief called deletion and annotation both doctrine-compatible, and they are not equally good. Deletion loses a distinction the crate elsewhere insists on keeping: a report from which an acknowledged block has vanished cannot be told from a report on a memo where no post-proof revision ever happened, and this is a tool whose no-rows path exists precisely to say that two states which happen to both be quiet are not the same state. The cost of printing is also already paid — the entry format carries an author's own reason verbatim today, under `revised because:`, with the source comment insisting it is never paraphrased and calling it the most actionable line the entry has.

So an acknowledged block moves rather than disappears. It leaves the group under the "prose revised after the claims it cites settled" preamble — which is what makes the acknowledgement feel like a discharge and not a footnote — and reappears under a single collapsed bullet listing, per block, its id, its line in the document, when it was acknowledged, and the author's own words for why. That collapse is the crate's own habit: the residue's preamble is itself one document-level bullet, adopted on the stated ground that a constant repeated per row buries what is specific to this document. Leaving the entry in place with an annotation stapled to it would keep the demand standing after it had been met, which is exactly the condition that teaches readers to skim the partition.
The acknowledgement, and the clause that had to go

The event records the block, the block's current text and citation list, a digest of each cited claim's proposition as it stands at that moment, and the author's verbatim reason; it carries a timestamp because every workspace event does. A listing is suppressed exactly when some ack for that block matches all of it, byte for byte, against values the check recomputes. Nothing derived is written down: the digests stored are the same `sha256_hex` of a claim's current proposition that the trigger already computes in order to decide what is in proof, so the ack stores an observation of the world at ack time and the check stores nothing at all.

The sketch also wanted the ack's timestamp compared against the recomputed anchor. Working through when that comparison could ever decide anything showed it cannot. The rule is only ever consulted for a block the trigger has already listed, and listing is precisely the statement that the block timestamp exceeds the anchor; the ack is appended afterwards, to an append-only log, by the same workspace and the same clock function that stamped the prose event. Barring a clock set backwards mid-session, the ack timestamp is above the block timestamp which is above the anchor, so the clause is true every time it is asked. Removing it is not a simplification for its own sake — it leaves the suppression predicate with no timestamp comparison anywhere in it, and so the acknowledgement, alone among the moving parts here, does not inherit the two-clock bound that the trigger's own preamble has to print.
Invariants, and the mutations that redden them

Three properties are worth stating as invariants with tests, and each has a specific mutation that should turn its test red. Any later edit to the block's text or citations voids the ack, since both are in the key — weaken the comparison to text alone and a citation-only revision, which TET-30 deliberately made list rather than clear, would slip through an old acknowledgement. Any change to a cited claim's proposition voids the ack, since the key carries that claim's digest — drop the digests and an acknowledgement survives a rewrite of the very claim the paragraph was read against. And a workspace with no acknowledgement log at all behaves exactly as it does today, because the line reader treats a missing file as an empty log; make that an error instead and every memo rendered before this design would stop checking.

Underneath those is the property that makes the rest cheap to reason about: the acknowledgement is a filter applied to the trigger's output, never an input to it. Every failure mode of an ack — stale, unmatched, malformed, absent — collapses to the same behaviour, which is TET-30's behaviour unchanged. The set of blocks the reader is asked to act on can only shrink, so the design cannot invent a demand; and the machine partition is untouched, because this residue was never one of its disjuncts and the ack changes only which entries fill it. It is worth being clear about what this does not buy: keying on claim digests does not close TET-30's conceded blind spot for prose that ships alongside a claim revision. It only stops an acknowledgement outliving the state it attested to.

The event records the block, the block's current text and citation list, a digest of each cited claim's proposition as it stands at that moment, and the author's verbatim reason; it carries a timestamp because every workspace event does. A listing is suppressed exactly when some ack for that block matches all of it, byte for byte, against values the check recomputes. One detail here is easy to get wrong and I got it wrong first: the digests are taken over the claim as `claims.jsonl` holds it, not over the ledger-derived proposition the in-proof test must use. Those two strings differ — rendering replaces embedded newlines with spaces and importing trims the cell — so keying the ack on the trigger's digest would make any claim with an embedded newline or edge whitespace permanently unackable, silently. Both sides of the ack's comparison read the same source, and the snapshot already ships it.
why: C8 was revised after F8 showed the two digest sources are not the same string; the paragraph asserted the ack stores the digest the trigger computes, which is exactly the mistake the revision fixes.

text: Minting it, and what the verb can and cannot refuse

The verb is `prose --ack <id> --why <text>`, on both front ends, built into the same shared request shape the CLI and the MCP server already funnel through so that neither can drift on which missing flag gets refused. Its refusals are the ones the existing prose verbs already make and no others: the block must exist, must not be a heading, must carry citations, every cited id must resolve to a claim, and `--why` must be non-empty — the last on literally the test that already backs the revise verb's insistence that revisions explain themselves. The sketch's assumption that `--why` be verbatim and required survives the test unchanged, and is the only thing here a human writes.

One refusal that might seem obvious is impossible, and it is worth saying why rather than leaving it to be rediscovered. The verb cannot decline to acknowledge a block that is not currently listed. An authoring workspace contains prose, claims, facts, targets and counters, and no evidence records whatsoever — grading records live beside the rendered memo — so at mint time there is no anchor to compute and no listing to consult. Nor is the refusal wanted: since the ack is a filter over the trigger's output, acknowledging a block that is not listed suppresses nothing and costs nothing.
The lifecycle across render

Because the residue is computed against a snapshot and the snapshot is written by `render --out`, an ack minted after a render is invisible until the next one. That sequencing is not new and it is not this design's to fix: everything the check sees about a workspace it sees through the snapshot. What is this design's to decide is whether the acknowledgement changes the memo's bytes, and it must not — the determinism of `render` in the workspace alone is what makes a drift finding mean anything. Keeping acks out of the rendered output turns the extra render from an annoyance into a useful signal: it rewrites the snapshot in place and leaves the document byte-identical, so the discharge lands in version control as a change to the record with no change to the argument. That is a true description of what an acknowledgement is.
Withdrawal, supersession, and an append-only log

Supersession asks nothing of the design. Suppression is existential over matching keys, so a later ack with a different key simply does not match and a repeated ack for the same key changes nothing; there is no state to reconcile. Withdrawal is different, and it has to exist. An author who acknowledged too quickly, then read the paragraph again and decided it really does outrun its claims, cannot always rewrite it on the spot — and if the tool gave them nothing to say, this design would have rebuilt its own defect one level up. So there is an `Unack` event, carrying a block id and its own required reason, and suppression requires a key-matching ack appended after the last withdrawal for that block. It names only the block because a key-mismatched ack is void already. Resolving that by position in an append-only log written one line per event, rather than by comparing timestamps, is what keeps the mechanism clock-free from end to end.
The implementation surface

Four symbols change, and the whole-worktree census of each is what lets that be said rather than hoped. The rule function takes the acks as a further input and returns two partitions instead of one list — a signature change whose blast radius is bounded by there being exactly one production call site, everything else being its own definition, its eighteen unit-test calls and prose about it. The findings field gains a sibling for the acknowledged partition. The snapshot manifest goes from nine entries to ten. The non-coverage list gains entries. Everything genuinely new — the event types, the log, the two verbs — lands in a new module that nothing yet refers to.

TET-30's memo ends its implementation-surface claim with a sentence this design falsifies: nothing new ships in the snapshot, no schema changes. A tenth file ships and a new event schema exists, and pretending otherwise would be worse than paying for it. What the payment buys is bounded. The cross-build divergence is one-directional, and `check` names the binary that produced every report it writes — a property the crate justifies on the ground that a report which cannot be attributed cannot be disbelieved — so two reports that disagree about one memo can be told apart by their checkers. The one thing that does not cover is a reader holding a single old report, who has nothing in it to suggest an acknowledgement exists; for them the answer is the log itself, which ships in the snapshot beside the memo and is plain JSON lines readable with no tetel at all.
What changes, and what it costs

Stated upfront, before the argument that gets there: the discharge is a new workspace event in its own append-only log, keyed on the block's current text, its citation list and a digest of each cited claim, which suppresses the listing exactly while all three still match what the check recomputes. A tenth file therefore ships in the snapshot and a new event schema exists — falsifying, deliberately, the sentence TET-30's memo ends its implementation-surface claim with. What the payment buys is bounded. A build predating the change never opens the new file and prints exactly the listing TET-30 shipped, so the divergence is one-directional: an older build over-reports, and can never suppress an entry a newer one would show. `check` names the binary that produced every report it writes, on the crate's own ground that a report which cannot be attributed cannot be disbelieved, so two reports disagreeing about one memo can be told apart by their checkers. The one thing that does not cover is a reader holding a single old report, with nothing in it to suggest an acknowledgement exists; for them the answer is the log itself, which ships beside the memo as plain JSON lines readable with no tetel at all.

Rewritten to work where it sits — an upfront statement of the whole change and its price — and its citations widened to the claims that actually carry each sentence (C8 for the mechanism, C4 for the degradation direction, C16 for the broken guarantee).

text: What the acknowledgement does not establish, and where per-citation attribution goes

Two lines are owed in the printed non-coverage list, on the list's own standard that a deliberate exclusion earns its own line because a refusal that fired reads too easily as coverage it never claimed. One: an acknowledgement records that a human said they re-read the paragraph against its claims, and nothing verifies that they did or judges whether the paragraph is faithful — after an ack, the tool's silence is the author's assertion and not the tool's finding. Two: an acknowledgement minted after the last render is not in the snapshot the check reads, and suppresses nothing until the memo is rendered again.

The advisory recommendation that per-citation attribution be folded into the ack rather than into the trigger is accepted, and it is worth being blunt that the fold does not go far. The residue's own non-coverage list already concedes that whether a paragraph was examined against an earlier-settled co-citation is answered by no listing, and the acknowledgement does not answer it: the ack is per block, its key records only that every cited claim's digest was what it was, and the sole place a per-citation judgement can live is inside the author's verbatim reason, which nothing should parse. So the acknowledged bullet prints the block's cited claim ids beside that reason, letting a reader pair the author's words to the citations themselves, and the non-coverage entry stays exactly where it is.
Migration, and one question left open

When the full obligation ledger lands, these events are the discharge records it would consume for this residue class, and the log moves into it unrewritten. That works because nothing in an ack is specific to the check it discharges: it holds a block id, a text, a citation list, a digest per cited claim, a reason and a timestamp, and none of the quantities the rule derives — not the anchor, not any claim's first proof, not the block timestamp, not even whether the block was listed. The general ledger needs the events as they stand plus a rule that reads them, which is a re-homing and not a rework.

One line on the separate question of warning an author when they revise prose whose claims have settled: this design does not settle it and does not depend on it, but it does change its economics, since such a warning today could name no act and afterwards could name this one. Whether it is worth building stays a measurement question, unanswered here.

text: Supersession asks nothing of the design. The withdrawal event was the sole exception, so it is gone, and the case it protected is not the case this design exists for: an author who now believes the paragraph is faulty can repair the paragraph, which voids the acknowledgement by changing its key. That is an honest act, and it is the one they should be taking.

text: Supersession asks nothing of the design. Matching is existential over keys, so a later ack with a different key simply does not match, and a duplicate ack for the same key cannot change whether a block is suppressed. Withdrawal is the harder question, and I have now been wrong about it in both directions. text: There is exactly one verb — `prose --ack <id> --why <text>`, on both front ends — and, as the section on withdrawal explains, deliberately no second one. text: There is a second thing each front end does that this verb must not inherit. That refusal has to be added, not assumed. Of the ack's five refusals only two already exist: the block must exist, and `--why` must be non-empty, the latter on literally the test that backs the revise verb's insistence that revisions explain themselves. text: So an acknowledged block moves rather than disappears. Because the reason and the timestamp are recorded but not keyed, more than one ack can match a block at once, and the entry prints the earliest of them: that mirrors the trigger's own use of the earliest event bearing the current wording, and it shows a reader the moment the discharge was first made rather than the latest restatement of it. text: Three properties are worth stating as invariants with tests, and each has a specific mutation that should turn its test red. text: Nine symbols change, and the whole-worktree census of each is what lets that be said rather than hoped.
